justification: The draft sentence 'the barbarian sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle' parses cleanly and self-evidently attributes the sound to drums in the forecastle; a reader needs no knowledge of the try-pot-skin detail to understand that drums are making a loud, barbarian sound, so the omitted explanation is atmospheric color rather than a load-bearing referential anchor.
source_quote: a crowd of her men were seen standing round her huge try-pots, which, covered with the parchment-like _poke_ or stomach skin of the black fish, gave forth a loud roar to every stroke of the clenched hands of the crew
draft_quote: the barbarian sound of enormous drums came from her forecastle

justification: The draft sentence 'Next day four whales were slain—one by Ahab' parses cleanly and conveys its meaning without confusion; the omitted philosophical framing about fortune's favourites and the Bachelor encounter is atmospheric and causal color, not a definitional clause whose absence leaves the sentence broken or a reference dangling.
source_quote: Not seldom in this life, when, on the right side, fortune's favourites sail close by us, we, though all adroop before, catch somewhat of the rushing breeze, and joyfully feel our bagging sails fill out. So seemed it with the Pequod. For next day after encountering the gay Bachelor, whales were seen and four were slain
draft_quote: Next day four whales were slain—one by Ahab.

justification: The draft sentence 'For that strange spectacle—the head turned sunwards—conveyed a new wondrousness' parses cleanly and makes complete sense on its own: a reader understands that a whale's head turning sunward is a strange spectacle that struck Ahab with new wonder, without needing the generalizing cetological gloss that it is observable in all dying sperm whales.
source_quote: For that strange spectacle observable in all sperm whales dying—the turning sunwards of the head, and so expiring—that strange spectacle, beheld of such a placid evening, somehow to Ahab conveyed a wondrousness unknown before.
draft_quote: For that strange spectacle—the head turned sunwards—conveyed a new wondrousness.

justification: The draft omits 'here, too, life dies sunwards full of faith,' which is the positive premise that 'but see!' rhetorically overturns; without it the adversative pivot is a broken logical construction with no preceding term to oppose.
source_quote: here, too, life dies sunwards full of faith; but see! no sooner dead, than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads some other way.
draft_quote: where for long Chinese ages the billows have still rolled on speechless and unspoken to, as stars that shine upon the Niger's unknown source; but see! no sooner dead than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads another way.

justification: The draft sentence 'In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun' parses cleanly and is self-contained: seeking intercession 'in vain' is a coherent and complete assertion on its own, and the dropped subordinate clause ('that only calls forth life, but gives it not again') is elaborative explanation rather than a definitional anchor without which the sentence breaks.
source_quote: In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun, that only calls forth life, but gives it not again.
draft_quote: In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun.

justification: The draft's 'but see!' is a broken logical pivot: it signals a contrast ('but') against a positive preceding clause, yet the immediately preceding draft sentence ends with the Niger's-unknown-source image, leaving no positive term for 'but see!' to reverse; the source's 'here, too, life dies sunwards full of faith;' is the required antecedent clause that makes the opposition grammatically and logically parseable.
source_quote: here, too, life dies sunwards full of faith; but see! no sooner dead, than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads some other way.
draft_quote: where for long Chinese ages the billows have still rolled on speechless and unspoken to, as stars that shine upon the Niger's unknown source; but see! no sooner dead than death whirls round the corpse, and it heads another way.

justification: The draft sentence 'In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun' parses cleanly and conveys a fully intelligible meaning on its own — the whale's appeal to the sun is futile — without the excised relative clause, which elaborates the reason rhetorically but is not structurally required for the sentence to stand.
source_quote: In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun, that only calls forth life, but gives it not again.
draft_quote: In vain, oh whale, dost thou seek intercedings with yon all-quickening sun.

justification: The draft sentence about the waif-pole parses cleanly and self-evidently describes a lantern-topped pole thrust into a dead whale's spout-hole casting light over the water, with Ahab and his crew present alongside it — a reader without source access is not confused or misled, because the nocturnal vigil beside a dead whale is fully intelligible from the draft's own text.
source_quote: The four whales slain that evening had died wide apart; one, far to windward… the windward one could not be reached till morning; and the boat that had killed it lay by its side all night; and that boat was Ahab's.
draft_quote: The waif-pole was thrust upright into the dead whale's spout-hole; and the lantern hanging from its top, cast a troubled flickering glare upon the black, glossy back, and far out upon the midnight waves, which gently chafed the whale's broad flank, like soft surf upon a beach.

justification: The draft sentence parses cleanly on its own: 'Handling his cabalistical toy' functions as a self-contained participial phrase, and the very first word of Ahab's speech ('Foolish toy!') immediately names and characterises the object, while 'Curse thee, thou quadrant!' later in the same unbroken quoted passage explicitly identifies it—so no reader is left without a referent.
source_quote: Then gazing at his quadrant, and handling, one after the other, its numerous cabalistical contrivances, he pondered again, and muttered: "Foolish toy!"
draft_quote: Handling his cabalistical toy, he muttered: "Foolish toy! babies' plaything of haughty Admirals … Curse thee, thou quadrant!"

justification: The draft sentence parses cleanly and its meaning is clear: the two expressions appeared on the Parsee's face as he glided away, and a reader without source access would not be confused or misled by the slight temporal compression, nor is 'Unobserved he rose' necessary to understand the departure.
source_quote: these passed over the mute, motionless Parsee's face. Unobserved he rose and glided away
draft_quote: A sneering triumph seemed meant for Ahab, a fatalistic despair for himself, on the Parsee's mute face as he glided away.

justification: The draft phrase 'A voice answered through an interval of blackness and thunder' supplies its own implicit question—answered presupposes someone spoke into the darkness seeking a presence—so 'Old Thunder!' reads clearly as a self-identifying reply without needing Starbuck's literal 'Who's there?' to precede it; a reader without source access encounters no broken reference or dangling construction.

The draft phrase 'he changed' is grammatically parseable and contextually clear: the immediately preceding clause describes Stubb slipping and catching sight of the flames, so 'he changed' reads naturally as a change in tone or manner before the new exclamation, and no reader would be confused about Stubb's physical position or direction.
source_quote: immediately shifting his tone he cried—"The corpusants have mercy on us all!"
draft_quote: flinching from a swash that jammed his hand; but catching sight of the flames, he changed: "The corpusants have mercy on us all!"

justification: The draft sentence 'Starbuck, going forward, pushed against Stubb. "What thinkest thou now, man?"' parses cleanly and reads as a straightforward question from Starbuck checking in on Stubb after the supernatural spectacle; the dropped clause about the cry differing from the song is atmospheric/characterization detail that sharpens the contrast but is not needed for the exchange to make sense, and Stubb's response about taking the flame as a sign of good luck follows coherently without it.
source_quote: "What thinkest thou now, man; I heard thy cry; it was not the same in the song."
draft_quote: Starbuck, going forward, pushed against Stubb. "What thinkest thou now, man?"

justification: The draft sentence 'Again the high tapering flames leaped with redoubled pallor' parses cleanly and conveys the flames' return without requiring the reader to know it was triggered by Starbuck glimpsing Stubb's face; the dropped material (Starbuck's exclamation and its trigger) is atmospheric/narrative color, not a definitional clause whose absence leaves the sentence broken or referentially dangling.
source_quote: At that moment Starbuck caught sight of Stubb's face slowly beginning to glimmer into sight. Glancing upwards, he cried: 'See! see!' and once more the high tapering flames were beheld with what seemed redoubled supernaturalness in their pallor.
draft_quote: Again the high tapering flames leaped with redoubled pallor.

justification: In the draft, Ahab speaks last ('and Ahab again spoke: …'), so 'Overhearing him' immediately after points to Ahab as antecedent, which is the opposite of the intended meaning; replacing 'him' with 'Starbuck' removes the ambiguity.
source_quote: Overhearing Starbuck, the panic-stricken crew instantly ran to the braces
draft_quote: Overhearing him, the panic-stricken crew ran to the braces—though no sail was left.
